seo.title: Blemish care and post-blemish marks | Mocha Vietnam
seo.description: Telling an inflamed spot apart from the mark it leaves behind — two phases needing two different steps, and why the wrong order slows both.

heading: Blemish care
lead: Two phases, two different steps: while the spot is inflamed, and after it settles but leaves a darker mark.

compare.heading: Two steps for two phases, not two alternatives
compare.intro: This is where people commonly get it backwards: applying a mark-softening product to a still-inflamed spot, then concluding it does nothing.

criteria.label: When to use
values: While the spot is swollen and red
After it settles, leaving a darker mark

criteria.label: How to apply
values: Dab on the spot, a pea-sized amount
Spread over the area or face, two to three pea-sized amounts

criteria.label: Main actives
values: Tamanu oil, Acnebusters 3%, BHA 0.5%, sulfur, zinc PCA

criteria.label: What it addresses
values: Pigment left behind once inflammation has gone

compare.footnote: If you only pick one: pick for the skin you have today, not for the outcome you worry about most. While a spot is inflamed, the mark-softening step is not yet its turn.

sections.heading: A post-blemish mark is no longer a blemish
body: A spot passes through two quite different phases. First inflammation: a congested pore, a red and swollen area. Then the consequence of that inflammation — the skin produces extra pigment where it was inflamed, leaving a darker mark once the spot itself has gone.

The two phases need different things. The inflamed phase needs something acting on congestion. The mark phase needs something acting on pigment — the same active family used for melasma, because underneath it is the same pigment problem.
Get the order wrong and both are slower: a mark-softening product on an inflamed spot does not settle it faster, and a spot gel on a healed mark only dries that patch of skin.

links.label: See how pigment works on the pigmentation line

sections.heading: Squeezing makes the mark deeper, not faster
body: How dark and how deep a mark ends up tracks fairly closely with how inflamed things were beforehand. Squeezing increases inflammation, so it deepens and prolongs exactly the mark you were trying to avoid.
With a deep spot that has no head, squeezing also pushes the contents downwards rather than out — which is how a spot becomes a depressed scar.
Plainly: no product on this site compensates for squeezing.

sections.heading: Marks darken in the sun too
body: This gets overlooked because people file post-blemish marks under “acne” rather than under “pigment”. But pigment is what they are, and UV drives them exactly as it drives melasma.
So someone applying a mark gel faithfully each evening but skipping sunscreen each morning is pulling in two directions — the situation the sun protection line describes.
It is also why the mark gel is designed for evening use.

faq.q: What about severe or cystic acne?
faq.a: That needs a dermatologist. Severe inflammatory acne, cysts, or breakouts lasting months are not something a topical product resolves, and waiting usually makes the resulting scarring worse.

faq.q: Do post-blemish marks fade on their own?
faq.a: Most fade over time, but how fast depends on how deep the pigment sits and on daily sun protection. Shallow marks may fade over a few months; deeper ones take considerably longer.
No. A depressed scar is a change in the skin's structure, quite unlike a mark, which is only pigment. No topical product fills a depressed scar — that is work for medical procedures.
